claims.claim: The book is less a history of House Targaryen than a portrait of how history is constructed in Westeros; readers leave with no definitive account.
claims.quote: no definitive account of what really happened
claims.page: House of the Dragon Misses One of the Best Aspects of Fire & Blood

claims.claim: Eustace's account is a sober recollection of the fall; Mushroom's is a deeply sensationalized look at Rhaenyra, and the pairing suits morally complex figures.
claims.page: House of the Dragon Misses One of the Best Aspects of Fire & Blood

claims.claim: Sara Hess: the book is three separate reporters saying what they think happened and contradicting each other, so nobody in it actually knows.
claims.page: House of the Dragon Writer Reveals How Fire and Blood's Unreliable Narrative Shaped the Series

claims.claim: Hess: it is men talking about what they think happened, and they are probably wrong.
claims.page: House of the Dragon Writer Reveals How Fire and Blood's Unreliable Narrative Shaped the Series

claims.claim: The book layers court documents, royal decrees and Grand Maesters' histories with two first-person eyewitness accounts (Eustace, Mushroom).
claims.page: House of the Dragon's Alternate History Is More Scandalous Than You Think

claims.claim: Mushroom's testimony was deemed so salacious that King Baelor ordered it burned, a suppressed-source motif familiar from real archives.
claims.page: House of the Dragon's Alternate History Is More Scandalous Than You Think

claims.claim: Gyldayn cites Mushroom claims the text notes as obviously false, yet no follow-up statement blunts them, so the lurid version lingers.
claims.quote: no follow-up statement serves to blunt

claims.claim: Gyldayn admits not everything written is accurate, that history has mixed with folklore and historians disagree on details.
Minor figures simply disappear from the record, plausibly because the chronicler did not think their fates worth writing down.
In The World of Ice and Fire, everything attributed to Gyldayn was written directly by Martin, while Yandel's words were written by Garcia and Antonsson.
claims.source: A Wiki of Ice and Fire, 'Gyldayn' (citing r/asoiaf AMA)
claims.quote: directly written by George R.R. Martin
claims.page: Gyldayn - A Wiki of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: The original WOIAF frame had Gyldayn's papers found with pages misplaced, destroyed, or damaged by neglect and fire, the lost-manuscript topos.
claims.source: A Wiki of Ice and Fire, 'Gyldayn'
claims.quote: damaged by neglect and by fire
claims.page: Gyldayn - A Wiki of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: Gyldayn's line on the dragon Tessarion shows the chronicler's habit of closing an unknowable with a rhetorical question.
claims.source: A Wiki of Ice and Fire, 'Gyldayn'
claims.quote: Who can know the heart of a dragon?
claims.page: Gyldayn - A Wiki of Ice and Fire

claims.claim: The frame is a historical summary compiled from primary and secondary sources by Gyldayn, who brings his own bias to the importance and likelihood of events, so the history is fluid.
claims.page: 6 Mysteries to Ponder After You've Finished George R. R. Martin's Fire & Blood

claims.claim: WOIAF's dedication to Tommen is written over the half-erased names of Joffrey and Robert, so the document displays its own revision history.
claims.page: 19 Strange Things Hiding in The World of Ice and Fire

claims.feature: fawning brevity for the reigning house
claims.claim: Yandel's page on King Robert is very fawning and very short, the courtier-historian's survival instinct made visible.
claims.quote: Yandel knows how this game is played.
claims.page: 19 Strange Things Hiding in The World of Ice and Fire
